title: Cantonese Steamed Fish
subtitle: steamed whole fish with ginger and soy
excerpt: A whole fish steamed over boiling water for just 8 minutes, then finished with a pour of hot oil over ginger, spring onion, and light soy. The definitive Cantonese cooking technique. Serves 4.
sourceNotes: Steamed whole fish with ginger and soy is the cornerstone of Cantonese cooking. It showcases the Cantonese principle that the best ingredients need the least intervention.

glossaryTerms.definition: Cooking food over, not in, boiling water. The steam cooks the food gently and evenly. In Cantonese cooking, fish is steamed for exactly as long as needed: overcooking by even a minute makes the flesh dry and rubbery.
A Cantonese finishing technique where very hot oil is poured over aromatics arranged on top of a cooked ingredient. The oil sizzles, half-cooking the garnish and releasing its fragrance.
The Cantonese philosophy that the highest-quality ingredients require minimal seasoning. For fish, this means the soy and oil serve as a condiment, not a mask.

. The fish must be very fresh: bright eyes, red gills, firm flesh. The
time is exact. Set a timer. Pull the fish at 8 minutes for a 600g fish.

finish is applied at the very last second. Have a separate small pan heating the oil on the hob while the fish is in the steamer. As soon as the fish comes out, arrange the ginger and spring onion and pour the smoking-hot oil directly over. The sizzle is half the dish.

items.prepNote: about 700g, cleaned and scaled. Use cod fillet portions if whole fish unavailable.
half sliced for steaming, half julienned for garnish
2 for steaming, 4 finely julienned for garnish

content.text: Score the fish 3 times on each side with diagonal cuts down to the bone. This allows steam to penetrate evenly.
Place the sliced ginger and the 2 whole spring onions on the plate or tray you will use in the steamer. Lay the fish on top. This lifts the fish slightly and lets steam circulate underneath.
Bring water in the steamer to a vigorous boil. Place the fish plate inside. Cover tightly. Steam for 8 minutes for a 600g fish. Add 1 minute for every additional 100g.
While the fish steams, mix the light soy, sugar, and 1 tablespoon of water in a small bowl. Heat the vegetable oil in a small pan until it just begins to smoke.
Carefully remove the fish from the steamer. Pour away the liquid that has collected on the plate. This liquid is watery and dilutes the final flavour.

Arrange the julienned ginger and spring onion on top of the fish. Pour over the soy mixture. Immediately pour the smoking-hot oil over the garnish. It will sizzle loudly. Add a few drops of sesame oil if using. Serve at once.

attrs.symptom: Fish flesh is dry and cottony
attrs.cause: Oversteamed. Even 1-2 minutes too long will dry out the flesh.
attrs.fix: Use a timer every time. A skewer inserted into the thickest part should meet slight resistance. If it slides in with no resistance, the fish is done.

attrs.cause: The fish was placed directly on the plate without a layer of spring onion or ginger underneath.
attrs.fix: Always place aromatics underneath the fish before steaming. They lift the fish and prevent sticking.

content.text: Steamed fish with ginger and soy is perhaps the most fundamental expression of Cantonese cooking. It appears at virtually every family meal in Guangdong province and Hong Kong, as well as across the Cantonese diaspora in Southeast Asia, North America, and Europe. Whole fish is preferred because it cooks more evenly and is considered more auspicious than fillets. In Hong Kong, restaurant quality is often judged entirely on the quality of this single dish.
